newsitem.title: USA: May factory orders fall as new-car sales slump.
newsitem.headline: May factory orders fall as new-car sales slump.

text.p: Slumping new-car sales helped put a damper on U.S. factory orders in May, a Commerce Department report showed on Wednesday, adding to signs of an industrial slowdown.

The surprisingly sharp 0.7 percent fall in orders to a seasonally adjusted $323.3 billion -- the second drop in the past three months -- was the final piece of economic data available to Federal Reserve policy-makers as they wrapped up a two-day meeting on interest-rate policy.
Not only did orders falter in May, after a 1.4 percent April rise and a 1.7 percent March falloff, but shipments of finished goods declined and order backlogs also weakened.
Inventories of finished products mounted in warehouses during May for the ninth month out of the past 10 as sales failed to keep up with output.
Analysts said that raised the likelihood of production pullbacks in coming months since businesses have grown adept at keeping stocks of goods in line with sales.

"This buildup of inventories will give way to a significant slowdown in inventory accumulation in future months," predicted economist Elliott Platt of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.

Overall economic growth slowed markedly in the second quarter from the first quarter's booming 5.9 percent annual rate, possibly to a pace as slow as 1.5 percent to 2 percent a year, which would help ease inflation fears.
Separately on Wednesday, a report from CNW Marketing/Research in New York showed auto sales plunged 11.4 percent in the last 10 days of June from the comparable period a year earlier.
Chrysler Corp. said on Tuesday its overall sales of new vehicles had softened for a fifth straight month in June.
The Commerce Department said orders for all types of durable goods, from cars to turbines and funiture, fell 0.7 percent to $175.9 billion in May after a 1.8 percent April increase.
Orders for nondurables like food and paper products also were down, declining 0.7 percent in May to $147.5 billion after a 0.8 percent rise in April.
Among key categories, transportation equipment orders declined 3 percent to $38.5 billion following a 2.8 percent rise in April.
Excluding transportation, factory orders were down 0.4 percent in May following a 1.2 percent rise in April.
Previously, the department said factory orders rose 1.2 percent in April, but it revised that up moderately.
Some slowing in factory orders was anticipated -- though the May drop exceeded forecasts substantially -- amid other ample signs of easing in manufacturing activity.

On Tuesday, the National Association of Purchasing Management said its June index of activity fell to 55.7 from 57.1 in May as new orders and production each grew more slowly. Any reading over 50 indicates an expanding manufacturing economy, though the pace was less robust last month than earlier in the year.
Total shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, decreased by 1 percent in May to $323.5 billion after a 1.2 percent increase in April.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, plunged 13 percent to $5.5 billion in May after a 27.5 percent jump in April.
Orders for nondefense capital goods, a measure of business's expansion plans, rose 0.4 percent to $43.9 billion in May after declining 1.7 percent in April.
Order backlogs were virtually unchanged at $522 billion during May, after two straight monthly drops of 0.3 percent.
Inventories of finished goods rose 0.4 percent in May to $443.3 billion after increasing 0.7 percent in April.
